text: FLIGHT-CONTROL SOFTWARE IS AN UNBROKEN CHAIN
textPreview: FLIGHT-CONTROL SOFTWARE IS AN UNBROKEN CHAIN

text:
Timing: 1 minute

Suggested visual:
A four-stage signal path—Require, Model, Verify, Evidence—sets the throughline for the course.

Speaker notes:
Welcome the new engineer and establish the scope: this is not a block-by-block product tutorial and not a complete certification course. It is a practical mental model for how a controls engineer works inside an aerospace Model-Based Design program. The central idea is that the Simulink model sits inside a governed evidence chain. A good control law is necessary, but it is not sufficient. The engineer must also understand where the behavior came from, how interfaces are controlled, how tests prove the requirement, and how results become reviewable life-cycle data. The pitch-rate-limiter example will reappear throughout the session so every artifact feels connected rather than abstract.

Key teaching points:
• Simulink is one part of a controlled software lifecycle.
• The course follows one behavior from requirement to HIL evidence.
• The target outcome is practical onboarding, not standards interpretation.

text: The same behavior can be discussed, simulated, reviewed, tested, integrated, and traced.
textPreview: The same behavior can be discussed, simulated, reviewed, tested, integrated, and traced.

text:
Timing: 1.5 minutes

Suggested visual:
An executable model at the center connects requirements, control design, simulation, and verification.

Speaker notes:
Explain Model-Based Design as a lifecycle pattern, not merely drawing blocks. The model is executable: it has time, data types, sample rates, state, interfaces, and observable behavior. Requirements can link to model elements; tests can stimulate the model; generated code can be compared with model behavior; the same interfaces can later connect to architecture and hardware benches. This shared representation reduces translation between a control-law equation, a software implementation, and a test procedure—but it does not remove the need for reviews, independent verification, or configuration control. The model’s formal role must be defined in the project plans: it may be a design model, a source model used for code generation, or another project-defined artifact.

Key teaching points:
• Model-Based Design keeps the model central across the lifecycle.
• Execution exposes dynamic behavior before hardware is available.
• The project defines the certification role of each model.

Speaker notes:
Connect the learner’s existing MATLAB knowledge to Simulink. MATLAB is ideal for calculations, data conditioning, parameter studies, optimization, and post-processing. Simulink adds an executable block-diagram representation of a dynamic system. The arrows are not simply a visual ordering of statements; they carry typed values over simulated time, and blocks may maintain internal state. In daily work the tools are tightly coupled: a MATLAB script may open a project, configure a model, run a test suite, analyze logs, and publish a report. Aerospace teams use Simulink because control laws, plant dynamics, sensor processing, mode logic, interfaces, and tests can be reviewed in a shared environment before flight hardware exists.

Key teaching points:
• Simulink is a block-diagram environment for dynamic simulation and Model-Based Design.
• Graphical data flow complements—not replaces—MATLAB scripting.
• Time, state, data type, and interface semantics are first-class concerns.

text: Version-control the whole configuration—not only the .slx file.
textPreview: Version-control the whole configuration—not only the .slx file.

text:
Timing: 2 minutes

Suggested visual:
A five-row project-file map distinguishes model, MATLAB, live code, test, and dictionary artifacts.

Speaker notes:
Walk through the file types the engineer will encounter. The .slx file holds a Simulink model. MATLAB .m files contain scripts, functions, or classes; projects often use them for automation and callbacks. An .mlx file is a binary live script or live function that can combine code, narrative, and inline output. An .mldatx file is a binary Simulink Test artifact. It can contain Test Manager test definitions, and exported result sets can also use the extension. Do not treat it as a text file; use Test Manager or supported APIs. Add .sldd because a data dictionary is frequently essential to controlled model data. A reproducible configuration includes the model plus its tests, dictionaries, scripts, referenced models, project settings, and tool versions.

Key teaching points:
• Know which files define behavior, data, automation, and evidence.
• .mldatx is binary and should be managed with supported tools.
• A model without its configuration is not reproducible.

name: text-102
text: BUS = interface contract     DICTIONARY = controlled design data
textPreview: BUS = interface contract     DICTIONARY = controlled design data

text:
Timing: 2 minutes

Suggested visual:
A hierarchy of library, block, signal, and subsystem sits beside a bus and data-dictionary interface example.

Speaker notes:
Define the core vocabulary. A block performs an operation: gain, filter, integrator, switch, lookup, saturation, state chart, or custom algorithm. Signals carry values between blocks and should have meaningful names, units, dimensions, types, and rates. A subsystem creates hierarchy and an interface around related behavior. Libraries provide controlled reusable blocks. A bus groups related signals through a port; it is valuable when the interface is defined by a Simulink.Bus object rather than by appearance alone. A data dictionary stores persistent design data such as parameters, bus objects, enumerations, and signal definitions. The point is not to hide complexity. The point is to expose it at the right level while keeping contracts controlled.

Key teaching points:
• Blocks express behavior; signals express data flow.
• Subsystems manage hierarchy and review scope.
• Buses and data dictionaries turn visual connections into controlled interfaces.

text:

Suggested visual:
An authentic export of the delivered closed-loop feedback model shows command, control, plant, sensor, feedback, and disturbance paths.







Speaker notes:
Use this loop as the mental map for most later diagrams. The pilot or guidance system provides a command. The controller compares commanded and measured behavior and produces an actuator command. Actuator dynamics and aircraft dynamics create motion. Sensor processing returns measured pitch, roll, rate, altitude, acceleration, or other states. Disturbances and uncertainty enter through gusts, aerodynamic variation, mass properties, failures, and latency. In Simulink, the plant model may be simple for a unit test and far more detailed for system simulation. The control-law model must be evaluated for stability, tracking, disturbance rejection, saturation, mode transitions, invalid data, timing, and interfaces—not simply whether one nominal plot looks correct.

Key teaching points:
• Feedback closes the loop from aircraft response to controller.
• The plant and sensors are part of the verification environment.
• The operating envelope and fault cases define the real test space.

text:
Timing: 2 minutes

Suggested visual:

Speaker notes:
Relate familiar control concepts to model patterns. A Gain block implements a scalar or matrix gain. Filters can be represented as transfer functions, discrete filters, state-space blocks, or explicit difference equations. Integrators represent continuous or discrete accumulation and require careful initial-condition handling. Lookup tables implement calibrated or scheduled behavior across operating conditions. Stateflow is commonly used for modes, guards, transitions, and fault logic. Saturation and rate-limiting blocks protect actuators and commands—but distinguish a magnitude limiter from a slew-rate limiter. Sensor processing often includes scaling, validity, filtering, voting, and unit conversion; actuator paths may include command shaping, rate limits, position limits, and monitoring.

Key teaching points:
• Choose blocks that preserve the intended mathematics and execution semantics.
• Scheduling connects one control-law structure to a changing flight envelope.
• Limits and mode logic are requirements, not cosmetic safeguards.

Contrast the loops without turning the slide into a control-theory lecture. Pitch and roll inner loops often regulate rate or attitude and drive control surfaces. Altitude hold is usually an outer loop that creates a pitch or vertical-speed command for an inner loop. The exact architecture varies, but the modeling discipline is consistent: explicit inputs and outputs, defined units and coordinate conventions, sample rates, limits, valid modes, scheduling variables, and fallback behavior. During model review, a sign error or unit mismatch can be more dangerous than a badly tuned gain, because a nominal desktop test may not expose it across every interface and mode.

Key teaching points:
• Nested loops turn high-level objectives into inner-loop commands.
• Interfaces and conventions must be reviewable at every loop boundary.
• Nominal plots do not replace boundary, mode, and fault verification.

Suggested visual:

Speaker notes:
Explain the separation of concerns. Mode logic decides whether a control law is off, armed, engaged, or degraded and specifies the guards for transitions. Stateflow is a common representation, but explicit Simulink logic may also be used. Scheduling changes gains or limits as functions of Mach, altitude, angle of attack, center of gravity, or aircraft configuration. A schedule is not a mode switch unless the requirement defines it that way; interpolation and breakpoint behavior matter. Verification must cover transition guards, persistence, priorities, temporal behavior, boundary points, extrapolation policy, and invalid scheduling data. The new engineer should never assume that a colorful state diagram or smooth lookup surface is self-explanatory—each transition and breakpoint needs requirements and tests.

Key teaching points:
• State machines govern discrete modes and transitions.
• Lookup tables adapt continuous behavior across the envelope.
• Transitions and breakpoints are first-class boundary tests.

name: box-194
text: The project plans define whether a model is specification, design, source, or verification material—and which objectives apply.
textPreview: The project plans define whether a model is specification, design, source, or verification material—and which objectives apply.

text:
Timing: 2 minutes

Suggested visual:
Two complementary columns separate the base DO-178C objectives from the DO-331 model-based supplement.

Speaker notes:
Frame DO-178C correctly. FAA AC 20-115D recognizes DO-178C and applicable supplements as an acceptable means of compliance for airborne software; it is not a regulation and not a product certificate. The standard is objective-based. It expects planned processes and evidence showing that applicable objectives are satisfied. DO-331 supplements the base guidance when models are used for development or verification. The project must define each model’s role because that determines which standards, reviews, verification activities, traceability, and tool considerations apply. Emphasize that generated code and automated tests can reduce manual effort, but automation does not remove responsibility for correct requirements, model standards, independent verification where required, configuration control, or credible results.

Key teaching points:
• DO-178C is an objectives-and-evidence framework.
• DO-331 applies model-based guidance alongside DO-178C.
• A model’s planned certification role controls how it must be verified.

[Sources]
- https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_20-115D.pdf
- https://www.rtca.org/do-178/


V3 terminology clarification:
- Prefer the training-example title “Gas Turbine Controls: Model-Based Development with Independent Verification,” not “independent compliance.”
- DO-178C is an accepted means of compliance, not a standalone software certificate. DO-331 supplements DO-178C for model-based development and verification.
- A Simulink model is not automatically compliant; its planned role, traceability, reviews, verification, configuration control, and lifecycle data determine what credit may be requested.

text: The system safety assessment assigns the software level; the controls team does not choose it for convenience.
textPreview: The system safety assessment assigns the software level; the controls team does not choose it for convenience.

text:
Timing: 2 minutes

Suggested visual:
A five-level ladder links Levels A through E to failure conditions and increasing assurance rigor.

Speaker notes:
Introduce the levels without turning them into arbitrary quality grades. The system safety process determines the effect of software failure and allocates the software level. Level A corresponds to a catastrophic failure condition, B to hazardous or severe-major, C to major, D to minor, and E to no effect. More safety-critical software must satisfy more objectives and greater verification independence. Avoid implying that every flight-control function is automatically Level A; allocation depends on system architecture and failure effects. For the engineer, the level changes review rigor, coverage expectations, independence, configuration evidence, and the acceptable use or qualification of tools. It never changes the basic obligation to implement the requirement correctly.

Key teaching points:
• Levels come from system safety analysis.
• Rigor increases as failure consequence increases.
• Software level affects objectives, independence, and evidence strategy.

[Sources]
- https://www.faa.gov/aircraft/air_cert/design_approvals/dah/software
- https://www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/Advisory_Circular/AC_20-115D.pdf


V3 software-level and independence clarification:
- Say “DO-178C Software Level A” when discussing software objectives. Use a broader system Development Assurance Level only when discussing the system-level allocation that informed the software level.
- Independence applies to designated verification objectives under approved plans. Avoid the blanket claim that an author can never participate in review; where independence is required, the author should not be the sole independent verifier of their own work.

name: box-236
text: Pipeline and test results are evidence inputs—not automatic approval.
textPreview: Pipeline and test results are evidence inputs—not automatic approval.

text:
Timing: 2 minutes

Suggested visual:
A bidirectional chain links requirement, model element, test case, and result above an evidence package.

Speaker notes:
Define traceability as a practical navigation system. Forward trace answers: where is this requirement implemented and how is it verified? Backward trace answers: why does this model element, parameter, test, or code path exist? Gaps can reveal missing tests, unintended functionality, or unreviewed derived behavior. Verification evidence includes more than pass/fail plots: approved plans and standards, review records, procedures, requirements-based results, applicable coverage and analyses, configuration records, quality records, and problem reports. A Jenkins job or HIL campaign can produce valuable evidence, but the project must control the configuration, link results to requirements, review failures and waivers, and retain the artifacts required by the plans.

Key teaching points:
• Traceability must work in both directions.
• Evidence includes reviews, analyses, configuration, and results.

Teach disciplined triage. Preserve the failing log, build identifier, commit, configuration, agent, and first meaningful error. Try the controlled local command rather than improvising a different workflow. If the failure does not reproduce, compare environment: MATLAB release, licensed products, project startup, path order, data dictionaries, environment variables, cached artifacts, and agent configuration. Speaker notes:
Turn HIL from a demo into verification. Functional tests connect inputs and outputs to requirement tolerances. Timing tests specify frame rate, latency, jitter, and overrun criteria. Interface tests verify scaling, units, freshness, status, protocol behavior, and electrical behavior as applicable. Fault tests inject realistic stale data, dropouts, resets, actuator failures, and power transitions and verify the required response time and state. text:
Timing: 1.5 minutes plus questions

Suggested visual:
A two-column close summarizes the lifecycle and gives the new engineer a practical first-30-days checklist.

Speaker notes:
Synthesize the course rather than repeating slide titles. Simulink makes dynamic behavior executable and reviewable. DO-178C and DO-331 place that behavior inside planned objectives and evidence. Good requirements define conditions, boundaries, interfaces, timing, and observable results. Unit tests, .mldatx organization, callbacks, architecture compile, Jenkins, and HIL each answer different questions; none replaces the others. Encourage the engineer to learn the local project by tracing one real requirement end to end, making one small controlled change, adding a boundary test, reproducing one pipeline failure, and watching how a HIL run is reviewed and retained. End with questions focused on the organization’s actual plans, standards, model role, toolchain, and evidence repositories.

Key teaching points:
• Correct control behavior and correct lifecycle evidence must stay synchronized.
• Each verification environment targets a different class of risk.
• The fastest onboarding path is one small end-to-end change under the project process.
